title: How much land does the farmer give in all?
description: A farmer gives the same part of an acre to each of five grandchildren, and the video finds the total by adding the same plot five times and counting the parts. Keeko then raises a hand with the doubt that the five should also multiply the bottom number.
teaching_notes: One idea: a whole number times a fraction gives that many pieces of the same size, so only the top number grows. Watch for students who multiply the whole number into both the top and the bottom and get a fraction that is just one plot again.

source: A farmer had 5 grandchildren. She gave 2/3 acre of land to each of them. How much land did she give in all?
video_script.why: The child has met a whole number times a fraction as repeated addition and now sees the same step give a total that is more than one whole acre.
video_script.substitution: Five plots of two thirds of an acre each make ten parts of one third of an acre.
video_script.anchor: A farmer gives two thirds of an acre to each of five grandchildren: how much land in all?
video_script.wrong_move: multiplies the five into both the top and the bottom of two thirds and gets ten fifteenths, which is only one plot again
video_script.payoff_line: The farmer gave ten thirds of an acre, that is three and one third acres, to her grandchildren

final_answer.spoken: ten thirds of an acre, that is three and one third acres

video_script.fraction_reading: two thirds, ten thirds, ten fifteenths
maths_rules: 5 × 2 = 10 parts of size 1/3, so the total is 10/3 acre
the slip: 10/15 = 2/3, the land of one grandchild
video_script.design: One idea: multiplying by a whole number counts more pieces of the same size. Five plots of two thirds of an acre stay on the stage as the anchor; the working band builds in the idea part.

beats.on_screen: small title card From your book; a farmer with five grandchildren in a row; a plot of 2/3 acre beside each one; a question mark over the whole row

marks.scene: the small title card From your book appears
marks.give: the five grandchildren and the plot of two thirds of an acre beside each one appear
marks.ask: a question mark appears over the whole row

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book about a farmer.
<bookmark mark='give'/>The farmer has five grandchildren. She gives two thirds of an acre of land to each one.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How much land does she give in all?

beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: one acre drawn as a square cut into three equal parts; two parts shaded as the plot of one grandchild; five such plots set side by side

marks.acre: one acre is drawn and cut into three equal parts
marks.plot: two parts are shaded as the plot for one grandchild
marks.five: five such plots are set side by side

narration: <bookmark mark='acre'/>Picture one acre of land, cut into three equal parts.
<bookmark mark='plot'/>Two of those parts make the plot for one grandchild.
<bookmark mark='five'/>Five grandchildren get five such plots, one after the other.

beats.on_screen: Given: land for each grandchild = 2/3 acre; 5 grandchildren

marks.given: the given lines are written in the working band

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, each grandchild gets two thirds of an acre, and there are five grandchildren.

beats.on_screen: To find: land given in all

marks.find: the find line is written under the given lines

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the land the farmer gives in all.
<bookmark mark='mult'/>Step one, five plots of the same size means we multiply.
We multiply five by two thirds of an acre.

marks.add: the five equal plots are written with plus signs

narration: <bookmark mark='add'/>Step two, five times a number means adding that number five times.
We write two thirds five times, with plus signs between.

marks.count: each plot shows two parts of one third

narration: <bookmark mark='count'/>Step three, each plot has two parts, and each part is one third.
<bookmark mark='ten'/>Five plots have five times two parts. Five times two is ten, so there are ten parts of one third.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>Ten parts, each one third of an acre, make ten thirds.
<bookmark mark='mixed'/>The farmer gave ten thirds of an acre, that is three and one third acres, to her grandchildren.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the answer
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: 5 × 2/3 = 10/15 is written and crossed out; a note shows 10/15 is the same as 2/3, the plot of one grandchild; five plots of two thirds are shown again

marks.fix: the note 10/15 = 2/3 appears and the line is crossed out
marks.rule: the five plots glow, and the bottom number is circled

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the answer is ten fifteenths of an acre.
Keeko multiplied the five into the top and the bottom.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But ten fifteenths is the same as two thirds of an acre.
That is the land for one grandchild, and not for all five.
<bookmark mark='rule'/>The five tells us how many plots we add. Each plot keeps its size, so the bottom number stays three.
